Tekion Spend offers the first fully-featured bank account native to an automotive dealer management system.

Please replace the release issued September 23, 2026, with the following corrected version due to multiple revisions.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260923757647/en/

The updated release reads:

TEKION, INCREASE, AND CORE BANK PARTNER TO BRING INDUSTRY-FIRST EMBEDDED BANKING TO AUTOMOTIVE RETAIL

Tekion Spend offers the first fully-featured bank account native to an automotive dealer management system.

Tekion, Increase, and Core Bank today announced embedded banking inside Automotive Retail Cloud (ARC). Built from the ground up as AI-native, ARC unifies all departments across more than 2,000 dealerships today. Tekion Spend, built on Increase in partnership with Core Bank, provides the first fully embedded banking solution designed for automotive dealerships.

Automotive dealerships are operationally complex businesses. Every year, a single dealership makes hundreds of thousands of payments to various suppliers, vendors, and customers. Until now, dealerships have had to make those payments outside of the software platform they use to run the rest of their business. Dealership staff have to manage an external bank account and print thousands of checks annually to make payments. Most still reconcile payments manually in their dealership management system at month end.

Tekion Spend solves this by embedding banking directly into ARC. Dealerships can now:

Open a fully-featured, FDIC-insured bank account in their name

Store and earn money on their deposits

Send money over any US payment rail and see exactly where it is at every moment

Reconcile payments in real-time

Manage every rooftop from one account

Increase makes this all possible via API, offering bare-metal infrastructure that gives Tekion full access to the Federal Reserve's data and capabilities, in partnership with Core Bank. Increase provides accounts and scaled accounts payable for Tekion Spend.

Accounts payable is the first step in Tekion’s larger plans for embedded banking. Dealerships move billions annually just to manage their floorplans. They also move money in service, sales, finance and insurance, and payroll. Today, each of those flows ends in a separate portal. Through Tekion Spend with banking powered by Increase, dealerships can soon manage the vast majority of their funds' flows from within ARC.

“Tekion Spend gives automotive dealerships a fully-featured bank account inside their existing system of record,” said Jamie Fox, GM of Fintech at Tekion. “It sees the invoice, the payment, and the ledger entry as one object rather than three systems reporting to each other after the fact. This is a natural step in Tekion’s mission to deliver end-to-end service for automotive retail.”

“Increase exists to help ambitious technology companies build great financial products,” said Jack Flintermann Reed, Head of Product at Increase. “We help our users get to market faster than they imagined possible. Prior to building the full product that’s launching today, Tekion built an initial working prototype on Increase APIs in less than three weeks.”

“Tekion has built an impressive platform and has a deep understanding of the operational needs of today’s dealerships,” said Lindsay Borgeson, President of Core X. “We are excited to partner with Tekion to bring even greater value to the automotive retail market and give their customers the confidence that comes from having their dealership funds held with a trusted, regulated financial institution. We believe this partnership will deliver meaningful value to dealerships and are thrilled about what we can accomplish together.”

Tekion Spend is available to US ARC dealerships beginning in Q4.

Tekion Spend banking products and services are provided by Core Bank, Member FDIC. Technology services are provided by Increase Technologies, Inc. Tekion is not a bank.

Tekion is redefining automotive retail with its end-to-end AI-native, platform purpose-built for the industry. By embedding AI into every workflow, Tekion delivers intelligent automation, real-time insights, and advanced decision support - driving efficiency, revenue, and modern consumer experiences. As the first and fastest cloud-native platform for automotive, Tekion brings OEMs, dealers, partners, and consumers together through its revolutionary suite: Automotive Retail Cloud (ARC) for retailers, Automotive Enterprise Cloud (AEC) for manufacturers and large automotive enterprises, and Automotive Partner Cloud (APC) for technology and industry partners. With AI-powered, cloud-native technology, Tekion enables the most seamless, transparent, and profitable retail experiences in the industry. For more information, visit www.tekion.com.

About Increase

Increase offers API-first banking for ambitious technology companies. Companies like Coast, Gusto, and Ramp rely on Increase technology to process more than $500B annualized in payments, card transactions, and loans. Increase built its own bank core technology from scratch: it’s transparent, reliable, and flexible so users can build great financial products on top. Increase has offered banking infrastructure since 2020 and introduced Increase Bank, Member FDIC in 2026. Learn more at increase.com.

About Core Bank

Core X, a division of Core Bank, is a technology-forward, solutions-driven financial institution built for fintech and Vertical SaaS companies that need more from their banking partner. Core X delivers a differentiated partnership built around speed to market, deep compliance expertise, strong risk management, and strategic support. Through our managed compliance model, partners can focus on growing their businesses while Core Bank provides the regulatory oversight and banking expertise to scale responsibly. data.full_text:
August delivered a wave of new fintech innovations, including new stablecoins and wealth management platforms. Here, we run through five of the top new launch stories from the month, featuring Revolut, Decade, the US Department of the Treasury, and more.

Revolut launches euro-backed stablecoin EURR

UK challenger Revolut has launched EURR, an Ethereum-based, euro-denominated digital token, marking the first stage of its stablecoin strategy.

Revolut, which serves over 80 million customers globally and boasts a user base of more than 16 million crypto users, has begun a phased rollout of EURR to eligible customers in Denmark, Poland, and Portugal, with "wider availability in other EEA markets expected later this year", the company says.

Revolut does not issue the token itself. Instead, Stripe's stablecoin infrastructure firm Bridge mints it under its newly secured MiCA Crypto-Asset Service Provider licence and Luxembourg Electronic Money Institution authorisation. Revolut's crypto arm, Revolut Digital Assets Europe, then integrates the token into the bank's consumer retail app.

Related:Lunar founders launch new AI audit company Repodo

Read more here

Ex-Nubank execs launch AI wealth manager Decade following $85m seed round

Decade, a Brazilian AI wealth management start-up, has emerged from stealth with $85 million in seed funding. The round, which Decade claims as the largest seed investment ever raised by a start-up in Latin America, was backed by Greenoaks, Benchmark, and Diffusion.

Based in São Paulo, Decade offers a financial wealth management platform that integrates custom financial AI models with human advisors to consolidate asset tracking, diagnose portfolio inefficiencies, and provide investment guidance.

Decade is the brainchild of former Nubank CTO Vitor Olivier and Felipe Meneses, founder of data intelligence firm Hyperplane, which Nubank acquired in 2024. Meneses subsequently spent a year within Olivier's technology unit as a machine learning engineer.

Read more here

Exclusive: Clayton Hayward steps down as EFT Corporation group CEO to launch AI venture Tharvos

Clayton Hayward is stepping down as the group CEO of EFT Corporation to create a new AI venture builder called Tharvos, FinTech Futures can exclusively reveal. Hayward announced the career move on LinkedIn, stating: "After 8+ years, my time as group CEO of EFT Corporation has come to an end."

Hayward is not departing the business in full. His departure statement further explains: "I'm not going anywhere as a shareholder in EFT, and I'll continue to support my co-founders Mike Smits, Paul Carter-Brown, and Jason Penton in an advisory capacity."

Related:Maltese start-up Mrkts debuts prediction markets infrastructure offering

Hayward has now come together with software entrepreneur George Gericke to create Tharvos. On his new company, Hayward's departure statement continues: "We invest in, build and operate AI-native ventures and we stand them up next to the industry leaders they're built to compete with."

He further elaborates to FinTech Futures: "We have already launched our first project, NIJA, a prepaid AI token platform similar to OpenRouter," adding that "We will launch several others before end of the year in insurance, longevity and wellness, and financial services."

Read more here

Former Stripe exec launches Increase Bank in US

US fintech Increase is launching a new FDIC-insured financial institution called Increase Bank. The entity combines regulated banking services with the financial infrastructure platform Increase has been building under founder Darragh Buckley since 2020.

Increase Bank will provide businesses with deposit accounts, payment services, and card issuing through the same API-based platform the fintech already offers to clients like Gusto, Ramp, and Stripe.

This platform serves as the system of record for customer balances and transactions at Increase Bank, and connects directly to payment networks including the Federal Reserve, the Clearing House, and Visa.

Related:Former MoneyLion execs debut wealthtech infrastructure venture Astraeus with $10m in total funding

Read more here

US Treasury launches Quantum-Readiness Task Force

The US Department of the Treasury has established the Quantum-Readiness Task Force to support the financial sector's "transition to quantum-safe technology in an orderly and operationally resilient manner", according to a launch statement.

The public-private initiative brings together technology providers, government bodies, financial institutions, financial market infrastructures, and other private-sector representatives to facilitate "coordinated preparation for quantum-related cyber risks".

The unit will focus on "practical, risk-based approaches to quantum readiness, including identifying critical dependencies, improving cryptographic agility, promoting interoperability, strengthening operational resilience, and addressing implementation challenges related to third-party dependencies and digital assets", the statement continues.

Read more here

data.ai_summary: Darragh Buckley, Stripe’s first employee, launched Increase Bank to improve the last mile of payment infrastructure by integrating banking systems with software companies. The initiative aims to enhance operational visibility and compliance, leveraging direct bank ownership to streamline payments, payroll, and data transparency. Buckley’s strategy focuses on making banking infrastructure more accessible and understandable for modern financial technology applications.

data.full_text:

Highlights Darragh Buckley went from Stripe’s first employee to bank owner with a contrarian bet: The biggest opportunity in payments sits inside regulated banking, not outside it. Increase Bank isn’t trying to rip out America’s payment rails. It’s built to fix the stubborn last mile between modern software companies and the bank infrastructure moving trillions of dollars. Buckley said richer data, continuous visibility and compliance designed into the software can reshape payroll, embedded finance and the meaning of community banking.

Watch more: Digital Shift With Increase’s Darragh Buckley

An engineer sits across the table from a bank examiner. How does that conversation go? Better than you might think, Darragh Buckley would argue. The engineer wants to know what the system is doing at every step. The examiner wants to know it’ll do the right thing every time. Those aren’t competing demands. They’re the blueprint for a better bank. That idea runs against one of FinTech’s founding stories: Banking’s future depends on replacing legacy infrastructure. But after helping build Stripe’s earliest banking integrations, Buckley reached a different conclusion. The rails weren’t broken. The trouble was the distance between those rails and the software companies trying to build on top of them. That conviction eventually carried Buckley beyond banking-as-a-service partnerships and all the way into bank ownership. Increase’s launch of Increase Bank is where that journey landed. Founder and CEO Buckley told PYMNTS CEO Karen Webster that his time as the first employee of Stripe revealed capabilities banks possessed but rarely exposed in ways modern software companies could actually use. “The systems are good and reliable,” Buckley said. “And they serve very much the use cases that they were built for.” But, he added, “many of our current use cases, especially around ambitious technology companies, run into edge cases that perhaps weren’t contemplated. If you’re rebuilding the technology stack anyway, contemplating those compliance regimes from the start makes it easier to build a safe and sound system.” Plenty of FinTech executives would happily send ACH and Fedwire to the museum. Buckley won’t. He credited the Federal Reserve with operating dependable systems. “The Federal Reserve is fantastically reliable,” Buckley said. “They changed the messaging format for Fedwire… across 3,500 institutions… and everything succeeded. Everyone got paid. Lights stayed on. Traffic still moved.” His analogy isn’t a blockchain or a rocket ship. It’s public transportation. The tunnels don’t change often. What riders feel are better schedules, easier payments and clearer explanations when something goes wrong. The infrastructure can stay put while the experience gets better. That mindset helps explain why Increase didn’t start by pursuing a banking charter. It first built its own technology stack, connected directly to payment networks, and developed the operations developers need to build financial products. Only after years of working with partner banks, serving on a community bank board, and learning how regulated banking really works did Buckley conclude that the final piece required owning a bank. The strategy grew out of the kind of operational frustration Buckley knew firsthand from Stripe. Take wire transfers. Sending the money usually wasn’t the hard part. Handling the exceptions was. A failed wire might arrive as an email demanding manual intervention, workable at dozens of transactions, painful at thousands. Buckley doesn’t blame partner banks. “They were built for a different kind of client,” he said. Software companies can’t treat payments as black boxes. They need to see when an instruction is received, transmitted and acknowledged. That status data can be as valuable as settlement itself because it’s what lets developers build dependable products around the payment. Buckley said. Webster put her finger on what buying a bank actually changed. “It seems like the bottlenecks come in many different ways, including the access part,” she said, referring to direct connectivity to Federal Reserve services and card networks. Buckley agreed, but direct access isn’t the whole story. Bank ownership also removes the final operational layer between payment networks and the businesses that depend on them. “Increase’s role is improving that last mile delivery as opposed to burning the house down and trying to build something new,” Buckley said. Data Turns Banking Into Software Fixing the last mile doesn’t stop at processing a payment. It means turning a bank’s operations into something software can see, test and trust. Consider Increase’s continuous test transactions that monitor connections to the Federal Reserve, Visa and other networks. Instead of waiting for customers to report a problem, the system keeps checking whether the infrastructure upstream is behaving as expected. Then there’s payroll, the invisible machinery of household finance. Buckley called payroll engineers “one of the great unsung heroes of the U.S. economy” because millions of consumers don’t think about payroll until it fails. Mortgages, rent payments and countless household obligations depend on those files arriving on schedule every pay period. “For most banks, that’s not the way it works,” Buckley said. “If you’re the payroll engineer, you send the instructions to your bank. Your bank may or may not turn around and say, ‘We got it,’ and that is the terminal point in that interaction. The next point you will know whether everything succeeded will be user support questions telling you, ‘I didn’t get my money.’” Increase answers the silence. As processing advances, it confirms receipt, submission to the Federal Reserve, and the Fed’s acceptance and action on the file. The goal isn’t simply faster payments. It’s knowing where the money is before support tickets start telling you where it isn’t. Buckley brings the same software lens to community banking. Community doesn’t have to mean geography, he said. Technology can group businesses by the financial problems they share. “The dentist in Bend [Oregon] looks more similar to the dentist in Boston than they do to the restaurant next door from a banking services perspective,” Buckley said. “We should end up with the bank for dentists, not the bank for Bend, Oregon.” That’s the engineer-and-examiner conversation in practice. Regulation supplies the guardrails; software makes the system visible. Buckley isn’t trying to tear banking down. He’s trying to make it legible to the companies building on top of it. Increase technology powers an API-first banking platform for ACH, check, and virtual card payments within VicPay, connecting the AP lifecycle from invoice ingestion through payment execution and reconciliation NEW YORK, Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Enterprise finance teams are moving from digitized workflows to autonomous finance operations, yet payments remain the most fragmented step in the AP lifecycle, often spread across separate providers, portals, and manual reconciliation processes. Vic.ai, the AI-native autonomous finance platform, today announced a partnership with Increase and Core Bank to power VicPay™'s account and payment capabilities. Increase’s technology is trusted by some of the largest fintechs and software platforms in the United States, providing flexible, transparent, and reliable tools for money movement, storage, and card issuance. Today, the Increase platform powers VicPay payments within the same environment where invoices are captured and approved. From approved invoice to settled payment For many AP teams, the handoff between invoice approval and payment execution is where visibility breaks down. By integrating with Increase technology, Vic.ai creates a seamless platform where approved invoices carry the customer's payment instructions, approval controls, and selected payment method through to execution, with funds moving through the customer's individual account at Core Bank before disbursement to vendors. Payment status and transaction information synchronize back into Vic.ai for tracking, exception handling, and reconciliation. The result is one unified operational loop rather than a patchwork of disconnected systems. Get the latest news

Customer funds are held in individual deposit accounts opened in each customer's own name at Core Bank, providing clear account titling and direct ownership of funds. The unified provider architecture strengthens the resilience of the VicPay platform and enhances its ability to support varied vendor requirements without manual workarounds. As across the Vic.ai platform, autonomy in payments operates under human oversight: approval hierarchies, user permissions, audit trails, and exception management remain in the customer's hands. Increase provides the banking infrastructure behind each payment rail and serves as the check payment provider for VicPay checks. Expert quote: "The value [for Buckley] comes from obtaining the institutional status and control that Increase could not fully achieve by relying solely on third-party banks." —Bank Slate Consulting's Paul Davis Darragh Buckley, founder and CEO of payment fintech Increase and one of Stripe's first employees, has officially launched his own bank. Buckley announced this week that Increase now has its own banking division called Increase Bank. The bank is a rebuilt conversion of Twin City Bank, a Washington-based community bank that Buckley acquired through buying its parent holding company last June. "Buckley bought a small bank to serve as the regulated chassis of a much larger tech business," Bank Slate Consulting founder Paul Davis told American Banker. "The value comes from obtaining the institutional status and control that Increase could not fully achieve by relying solely on third-party banks." Fintechs buying banks has been a part of the bank M&A scene for a while, but this deal involved a fintech entrepreneur buying a community bank's regulatory infrastructure for a custom rebuild rather than layering APIs on top of a conventional bank operating model. "By acquiring Twin City Bank, Buckley obtained an existing charter, FDIC insurance, a regulated legal entity, payment-system access and an institution with an exam history," Davis said. "The acquisition still required extensive scrutiny, but it provided a functioning banking chassis." Davis also noted that Twin City Bank was "big enough to have institutional infrastructure but small enough that Buckley didn't inherit a big branch network or legacy balance sheet to unload or unwind." Buckley initially filed a request to purchase 100% of Twin City Bancorp's voting shares in April of last year, according to Federal Register archives . The deal was subsequently permitted by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco two months later. Twin City Bank had $70 million in assets under management when Buckley initially filed to acquire it via the holding company share purchase, according to its FDIC call reports . By the time it rebranded to Increase Bank a year later, its asset size had grown 48% to $114.5 million, with the largest single-quarter increase (40%) occurring between Q4 2025 and Q1 2026. The community bank has one physical branch in Longview, Washington, which continues to do business under the Twin City Bank name according to the branch's website . Increase Bank "is a bank built by a team of product-obsessed operators for ambitious companies that are just as obsessed with building the best possible products for their customers," Buckley said in a statement. Fintech and banking consultant Annie DeStefano told American Banker that as the financial services ecosystem is growing, fintechs are exploring different ways to work with community banks. "New strategic options and paths will emerge," she said. "There is space for all the model types to work together, but the map will be redrawn [with] new specificity about which models make sense where." Increase, founded in 2020 by Buckley after his departure from Stripe, offers money movement APIs to fintechs such as Ramp and Stripe. A company spokesperson confirmed with American Banker that Increase gained its own Federal Reserve master account through acquiring Twin City Bank, which has a master account according to Federal Reserve records. data.full_text:
Fintech builders who route payments through Stripe, Ramp, or Gusto have been moving money through Increase's rails for years without knowing it. On Wednesday, the company behind that infrastructure did something the BaaS sector has talked about but rarely executed: it became the bank.

Increase launched Increase Bank — a federally regulated, FDIC-member institution — by acquiring and rebuilding Twin City Bank of Longview, Washington, into a purpose-built fintech infrastructure bank. The result collapses the three-layer structure that has defined banking-as-a-service for a decade, and that regulators have spent the past two years trying to police. There is no longer a sponsor bank on one side and a technology provider on the other. Increase is now both.

For fintech builders, that architectural change has a concrete implication: they can access payment rails, FDIC deposit accounts, and a real-time reconciling ledger through a single regulated entity — without stitching together a relationship with a sponsor bank and a separate API provider, and without the compliance handoffs between them that produced the Synapse disaster.

How BaaS Builds the Middle Layer That Keeps Breaking

The standard banking-as-a-service arrangement has always had a structural seam. A fintech facing the end customer, a middleware provider handling ledger management and API connectivity, and a chartered sponsor bank holding the regulated relationship — three entities, three ledgers, three sets of compliance obligations, and a cascade of third-party dependency that regulators have characterized as fundamentally difficult to supervise.

In July 2024, the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC issued a joint statement flagging heightened risks in bank-fintech arrangements — risks that arise specifically when banks rely on partners to manage customer-facing activities. That statement came after a torrent of BaaS-related enforcement actions in early 2024, following which analysts at Klaros Group predicted that virtually every bank with a BaaS or embedded finance line of business would face some level of regulatory action. The core regulatory complaint was consistent: a fintech cannot outsource regulatory credibility to its sponsor bank, and the bank remains responsible for the customer-facing activity delivered through third parties — even when it cannot see or control what that third party's ledger says.

The specific mechanical failure that produced the Synapse bankruptcy illustrates why. When Synapse — the middleware provider at the center of dozens of fintech-bank arrangements — collapsed in 2024, neither the partner banks nor the fintech apps could resolve a ledger discrepancy that stranded an estimated 100,000 consumers and locked them out of their accounts. The discrepancy existed because Synapse maintained its own ledger, the partner banks maintained theirs, and the two did not agree. There was no authoritative single record.

What Increase Bank Does Differently at the Architecture Level

Increase has connected directly to the Federal Reserve since its founding in 2020 — not through an intermediary bank — which means its core has always been the system of record for account balances and transactions. That direct connection is what makes the bank charter a structural completion rather than a strategic pivot.

Increase Bank's technology maintains the system of record for account balances and transactions and reconciles to the Federal Reserve in real time. There is no middleware ledger that can diverge from the bank's records, because the bank and the technology are the same entity. A fintech client's account events are recorded once, in one ledger, held by one FDIC-member institution that also maintains direct connections to FedACH, Fedwire, Check 21, The Clearing House's Real-Time Payments network, FedNow, and Visa.

That architecture answers the specific failure mode the Synapse collapse made visible. The reconciliation gap that stranded 100,000 consumers was a ledger divergence problem — three entities maintaining separate records that could disagree. With Increase Bank, there is one entity and one record.

The combination also changes what a fintech client can do from day one. Karim Atiyeh, co-CEO of Ramp, described the operational difference in the bank's launch materials: "From the ability to open accounts synchronously, fully featured for every payment rail, from day one to the pace they ship new features, Increase just gets it." Synchronous account opening — an account that exists the moment an API call returns, rather than after a back-office process runs — is an architectural capability, not a product decision. It requires that the ledger and the charter be under the same roof.

Darragh Buckley's Methodical Path From Stripe to Bank Founder

The path from infrastructure provider to chartered bank ran through Twin City Bancorp, Inc., a small community bank holding company in Longview, Washington, about an hour north of Portland, Oregon. In April 2025, Buckley filed a change in bank control notice with the Federal Reserve Board, disclosing the acquisition of voting shares in Twin City Bancorp — a transaction that required FDIC approval before closing. The deal received FDIC non-objection for control and closed, and the renamed institution is now Increase Bank.

The acquisition was Buckley's third investment in a Washington community bank. That detail matters: Twin City Bank, with assets of approximately $75 million and a single branch, was a deliberately modest acquisition target — not a platform with an existing BaaS book of business to integrate, but a charter, an FDIC certificate, and a clean regulatory record with a Satisfactory Community Reinvestment Act rating.

Buckley's motivation traces directly to his time as Stripe's first employee, where he spent six years building and scaling Stripe's bank partner relationship with Wells Fargo and designing the programmatic controls for deposit account structures, money movement, regulation, cybersecurity, and privacy. The lesson he took from that work: when you are simultaneously solving business, technical, and risk problems, you need to drop down a layer. At Increase, dropping down a layer meant connecting directly to the Federal Reserve instead of relying on an intermediary bank to hold those connections. At Increase Bank, it means owning the intermediary entirely.

Increase became profitable in 2025, remains self-funded, and processed hundreds of billions of dollars annually across ACH, wires, RTP, FedNow, checks, and cards before the bank charter was added. Monthly payment volume tripled year over year. The company referred overflow business to competitors — including Grasshopper Bank and First Internet Bank of Indiana — rather than take on clients it could not serve well. That restraint is what makes the charter announcement legible as a natural evolution rather than an opportunistic pivot.

What the Charter Costs, and Why That Matters

Owning a bank charter is not a cost-free architectural upgrade. The same regulatory framework that gives Increase Bank its compliance credibility now imposes obligations that a pure-software BaaS provider does not face.

As an FDIC-member institution, Increase Bank is subject to regular safety-and-soundness examination, capital adequacy requirements, and full Community Reinvestment Act obligations — not just the contractual compliance commitments a fintech makes to a sponsor bank. Capital requirements constrain how quickly the bank can grow its balance sheet. CRA obligations require documented investment in the communities it serves. And regulatory examination means a federal agency now has direct access to the bank's records and operations, not just to its sponsor bank partner's records.

That tradeoff is the specific cost of eliminating the compliance handoff problem. A sponsored fintech can structure its relationship to minimize regulatory surface area. Increase Bank cannot. Whether that constraint produces a competitive disadvantage or a durable credibility advantage will depend on how the regulatory environment for BaaS alternatives evolves over the next several years. The sector that will watch that answer most closely is the one that just watched Synapse demonstrate what happens when the unregulated middle layer fails.

Diede van Lamoen, former Head of International at Stripe and an Increase advisor, framed the competitive stakes plainly: "A fintech company's ability to scale often comes down to whether they have a banking partner that can move at their pace, build solutions to the edge cases they are solving, and give them direct access to payment rails." The question the market will answer over the next two to three years is whether "banking partner" and "banking infrastructure" are more valuable when they are one entity subject to a single regulator — or whether the operational discipline the charter imposes makes Increase Bank slower to move than a lighter-weight BaaS competitor.

What Comes Next for a Sector Sorting Out Its Architecture

The fintech sector generated more than $650 billion in revenue in 2025 and grew at approximately 21% annually, according to McKinsey data cited in Increase's launch materials. That growth has happened almost entirely on top of the three-layer BaaS architecture the sector is now reassessing.

Increase is not the only fintech to pursue vertical integration through a bank acquisition. Column Financial Technologies, founded by William Hockey of Plaid, took the same approach with Northern California National Bank in 2021 and has built a national-charter-backed API banking infrastructure serving clients including Mercury and Brex. Lead Bank in Kansas City followed a similar trajectory under former Block executives. The common thread in each case is the same architectural insight Increase articulates: the compliance problem in BaaS is not a process problem that better contracts can fix — it is a structural problem that requires owning the regulated layer, not partnering with it.

What Increase Bank represents, in the context of an industry sorting out which BaaS models survive sustained regulatory pressure, is a data point: the charter-acquisition path is executable, and it is executable by a company that built its reputation specifically on engineering discipline and financial soundness rather than growth at speed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between Increase Bank's model and standard banking-as-a-service?

Standard BaaS involves three separate entities: the fintech serving end customers, a middleware provider managing ledger and API connectivity, and a chartered sponsor bank holding the regulated relationship and deposit insurance. Each layer maintains its own records. When those records diverge — as they did in the Synapse bankruptcy — neither the bank nor the fintech has a clean path to resolution. Increase Bank collapses those three layers into one: Increase is the technology provider and the chartered FDIC-member bank simultaneously. Its core maintains a single system of record that reconciles directly to the Federal Reserve in real time, with no intermediate ledger that can diverge.

What happened with Synapse, and why does it matter here?

Synapse Financial Technologies was a BaaS middleware provider whose 2024 bankruptcy exposed a structural failure in the layered model: when Synapse's ledger diverged from its partner banks' records, approximately 100,000 end users were locked out of their accounts, with an estimated shortfall of $65 to $96 million. No single entity had an authoritative record of who was owed what. The Synapse failure demonstrated that the middleware layer in a BaaS arrangement carries a specific systemic risk — ledger divergence — that no amount of contractual language between the parties can fully resolve. Increase Bank's architecture eliminates the middleware layer, removing the divergence risk at its source.

Is owning a bank charter purely an advantage for a fintech company, or does it come with constraints?

Both. The charter gives Increase Bank regulatory credibility, direct payment rail access, and a single reconciling ledger — advantages that pure-software BaaS providers cannot match. But it also subjects Increase to capital adequacy requirements that constrain balance sheet growth, Community Reinvestment Act obligations that require investment in served communities, and direct regulatory examination by the FDIC. A partner-model BaaS provider can structure its operations to minimize regulatory surface area in ways a chartered bank cannot. Whether the credibility advantage outweighs the flexibility constraint is the competitive question the next several years of operating data will answer.

Who does Increase Bank currently serve, and what payments can it handle?

Increase's existing clients include Gusto, Ramp, and Stripe — companies that move money at scale across a range of payment types. Through Increase Bank's direct connections, it can process ACH transfers, wire transfers, Real-Time Payments via The Clearing House, FedNow transactions, check transfers under Check 21, and card issuance through Visa — all via a single API and a single chartered institution. The bank's FDIC membership and Federal Reserve connections were in place operationally before the charter conversion, meaning clients did not need to rebuild integrations when Increase Bank launched.

The obvious question is why someone building next-generation banking infrastructure would invest in legacy institutions that exist in a town an hour north of Portland. The less obvious question, which is the more interesting one, is whether Buckley is doing something most fintech founders don't bother with: learning what the actual plumbing of banking looks like from the inside, rather than from the outside looking in. Most fintechs treat banks as black boxes. You build an API, you find a partner bank that will lend you its charter, you share revenue, and you hope the compliance layer doesn't blow up. The way to build software that improves an industry is not to read about it from the top. It's to look at the smallest instance of the problem and see what's actually broken. Buckley has said publicly that he envisions a future where community banks serve specific communities - dentists, families managing elderly parents' finances, local businesses that still need a relationship with someone who understands their cash flow. That's not a sexy vision. It doesn't read well in a pitch deck. But it's also not wrong. Community banks hold roughly a quarter of U.S. banking deposits, and they're the ones that will need to modernize or lose their customers to whoever figures out how to serve them digitally without killing the relationship model. The Twin City investment sends a signal, but not the one the competitor-funded PR campaign apparently tried to paint. This isn't about Increase trying to own a bank. Buckley's been clear about that. # **Introducing Increase Bank, Built on the Infrastructure Powering Hundreds of Billions in Money Movement**

Share

---

*Increase Bank gives fintechs a regulated banking partner purpose-built for how modern companies operate: programmable, direct, and built to scale*

BEND, Ore.--([BUSINESS WIRE](https://www.businesswire.com))--Announcing the launch of Increase Bank, bringing a modern bank core together with regulated banking services to help teams build the best financial products with greater speed, precision, and control. Founded in 2020, [Increase’s banking infrastructure](https://cts.businesswire.com/ct/CT?id=smartlink&url=https%3A%2F%2Fincrease.com%2F%3Futm_source%3Dpressrelease%26utm_medium%3Dpressrelease%26utm_campaign%3DBankLaunch1%26utm_id%3DBankLaunch1%26utm_term%3Dincreasebank&esheet=54577876&newsitemid=20260729315404&lan=en-US&anchor=Increase%27s+banking+infrastructure&index=5&md5=dc38e27e29e0486455175b6e347863d6) and APIs enable companies like Gusto, Ramp, and Stripe to move, store, and lend hundreds of billions of dollars. With the addition of Increase Bank, an FDIC-member institution, fintech companies now have access to a bank engineered for their needs.

> “This is a bank built by a team of product-obsessed operators for ambitious companies that are just as obsessed with building the best possible products for their customers,” said Darragh Buckley, founder of Increase.
>
> Share

“This is a bank built by a team of product-obsessed operators for ambitious companies that are just as obsessed with building the best possible products for their customers,” said Darragh Buckley, founder of Increase. “It is programmable at scale and designed for reliability, speed, and flexibility.”

The idea for Increase was born out of Buckley’s experience building Stripe from its earliest days, where he saw the need for banking infrastructure built with the same engineering depth as the fintechs relying on it. Since that time, the fintech industry has become one of the fastest-growing sectors in technology, generating over [$650 billion in revenue in 2025](https://cts.businesswire.com/ct/CT?id=smartlink&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.mckinsey.com%2Findustries%2Ffinancial-services%2Four-insights%2Fthe-next-age-of-fintech-ai-digital-assets-and-new-paths-to-success&esheet=54577876&newsitemid=20260729315404&lan=en-US&anchor=%24650+billion+in+revenue+in+2025&index=1&md5=12fb60b27902383d5060f58f50063c16) and growing at about 21 percent year over year.

Increase now includes Increase Bank and a modern banking core with direct connections to the Federal Reserve, The Clearing House, and Visa. Increase’s technology maintains the system of record for account balances and transactions and reconciles to the Federal Reserve in real time. This gives fintechs full control over accounts and enables them to operate with their bank at the same speed and scale at which they operate their business.

“A fintech company’s ability to scale often comes down to whether they have a banking partner that can move at their pace, build solutions to the edge cases they are solving, and give them direct access to payment rails,” said Diede van Lamoen, former Head of International at Stripe and advisor. “Increase was built by people who have first-hand experience with these challenges and a drive to support users from the first payment to their billionth.”

Increase’s technology is trusted by some of the largest fintechs and software platforms in the United States, providing flexible, transparent, and reliable primitives for money movement, storage, and card issuance.

“At Ramp, we are building AI for finance, and we must move fast to save our customers' most valuable resources - time and money. Increase provides the banking infrastructure we need to do just that. From the ability to open accounts synchronously, fully featured for every payment rail, from day one to the pace they ship new features, Increase just gets it,” said Karim Atiyeh, Ramp's Co-CEO.

Visit [increase.com](https://cts.businesswire.com/ct/CT?id=smartlink&url=http%3A%2F%2Fincrease.com&esheet=54577876&newsitemid=20260729315404&lan=en-US&anchor=increase.com&index=3&md5=9aeb0c2eb88e29bf4ccbedb45df4cbb2) for more information.

**About Increase**

Increase combines modern infrastructure and banking to help teams building financial products move faster, with greater precision and control. Increase powers money movement, money storage, and card issuing with flexible, transparent, and reliable primitives so teams can build and scale with confidence. Increase’s core technology facilitates the movement of hundreds of billions of dollars in payments each year for leading companies such as Gusto, Ramp, and Stripe. Learn more at [increase.com](https://cts.businesswire.com/ct/CT?id=smartlink&url=https%3A%2F%2Fincrease.com%2F&esheet=54577876&newsitemid=20260729315404&lan=en-US&anchor=increase.com&index=4&md5=66f63562b63d308377ddac008d6887a8).

Banking products and services are offered through Increase Bank and Increase’s bank partners, each Member FDIC. Technology services are provided by Increase Technologies, Inc., a non-bank company.
